name: Frankincense

card.summary: An aromatic tree resin from Boswellia trees, used for centuries as incense and in perfumery, and in oils and extracts that people use for scent and skin or joint comfort.
card.note: Can cause allergic reactions; rare case report of mania with resin use.

quick.overview:
Frankincense is the dried resin of Boswellia trees. It is burned as incense, steam-distilled into an essential oil with a resinous, woody, spicy scent, and extracted into products containing boswellic acids.

For appearance, the most direct use is fragrance and skincare oils, where its scent is part of grooming. Indirectly, people take or apply Boswellia extracts for joint comfort, which they hope supports training and recovery. Research on it is mostly on joints and inflammation, not looks.
quick.how: People use it as incense, as a scented essential oil diluted in a carrier oil for massage or skin products, in perfumes, or as oral Boswellia supplements. Steam-distilled oils do not contain boswellic acids, though solvent extracts can.
quick.risks: Allergic reactions are described in the medical literature, and a published letter reports mania associated with Boswellia resin use. A 2008 systematic review noted no serious safety issues in the trials it covered. Trees are also over-harvested in some regions.

lead: Frankincense, also called olibanum, is an aromatic resin harvested from Boswellia trees. Its name comes from Old French for "true incense". It was traded across the Arabian and Somali peninsulas for centuries and appears in the Ebers Papyrus. [1]

In grooming it appears mainly as a scent: steam distillation gives an essential oil rich in monoterpenes such as alpha-pinene and limonene, used in perfumery and in massage and skin oils. [1] Solvent extracts contain boswellic acids, triterpenoids studied for anti-inflammatory activity. [1][2]

Reviews describe analgesic, tranquilising and antibacterial properties and report that Boswellia extracts reduce inflammatory conditions; a 2008 systematic review of seven randomised trials found clinical effectiveness in conditions such as asthma, osteoarthritis and Crohn's disease. [2][3]

angle.text: Frankincense contributes a woody, resinous scent to perfumes and skin oils. Some users also take Boswellia extracts for joint comfort, hoping to keep training; this is a chain through recovery rather than a direct change in appearance.

paras: Frankincense is the resin of Boswellia trees. By weight it contains gum (30 to 36 percent) and oils; a review lists terpenes including mono- and diterpenes, with the most biologically active being boswellic acid derivatives such as 11-keto-beta-boswellic acid. [1][2]

Several Boswellia species yield frankincense: B. sacra (Somalia and southern Arabia, with B. carteri now treated as a synonym), B. frereana and B. occulta (Somalia), B. serrata (India) and B. papyrifera (Ethiopia, Eritrea, Sudan).[1][13] About 90 percent of world production comes from the Horn of Africa.[1]

Trees begin producing resin at around 8 to 10 years old and are tapped two to three times a year; the final taps are described as giving the best resin, and more opaque resin is generally graded higher.[1] The resin contains gum (30 to 36 percent), acid resin, boswellic acids and incensole acetate, while the steam-distilled oil is about 75 percent monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes and ketones, led by alpha-pinene, limonene and beta-pinene, and contains no boswellic acids.[1] B. serrata contains beta-boswellic acid, acetyl-beta-boswellic acid, 11-keto-beta-boswellic acid and its acetyl derivative.[13]

Egyptian references to incense from the land of Punt date to the third millennium BCE, and the Ebers Papyrus (c. 1500 BCE) is among the earliest evidence of frankincense as a remedy.[1] Herodotus wrote that it was harvested in southern Arabia, Pliny the Elder mentioned it, and it appears in Exodus, in Jeremiah 6:20 as an import from Sheba, and in Matthew 2:11 among the magi's gifts.[1]

Frankincense was used in the Roman Empire, was reintroduced to Western Europe possibly by Frankish Crusaders and became common in Catholic Mass.[1] In the 13th century Zhao Rugua described it as traded to China from Arabian ports.[1] In 2000 UNESCO inscribed Oman's Land of Frankincense as a World Heritage Site.[1] In Ayurveda, the NCCIH notes, Boswellia resin was traditionally used for arthritis, inflammation and pain.[12]
Distilled oil has a resinous, woody, spicy scent and is used in perfumery. Massage oils combining frankincense and myrrh have been used in trials on comfort and pain. [1][4][5]
Traditional use stretches back to ancient Egypt. Modern reviews report anti-inflammatory action through inhibition of 5-lipoxygenase and reduced leukotriene release. [2][6]

Allergic reactions to incense and resin products have been reviewed by allergists. [7] A letter in the American Journal of Therapeutics reported mania associated with Boswellia resin. [8] The 2008 systematic review noted no serious safety issues in the trials it covered. [3]

A 2008 BMJ systematic review identified seven randomised trials of Boswellia serrata extract (asthma, rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease, osteoarthritis, collagenous colitis); all reported clinical effectiveness and three were of good quality. [3]

More recent randomised trials have examined a topical frankincense oil for knee osteoarthritis, frankincense and myrrh oil massage for chronic low back pain and for back pain before a cardiac procedure, and a frankincense-based product for urinary incontinence. [4][5][9][10] A Phase II COVID-19 study tested a curcumin-frankincense formulation. [11] None of these studied facial appearance.

The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health summarises research on Boswellia as mostly small studies; it reports that oral use may reduce inflammation and pain in osteoarthritis, that evidence for topical use in arthritis does not show effectiveness, and that clinical trials have used up to 1,000 mg daily safely for up to six months.[12] Wikipedia's page on B. serrata notes that osteoarthritis studies show slight improvement in pain and function.[13]
The page for the resin notes population decline of Boswellia trees from over-tapping and land clearance, with a predicted 50 percent drop for B. papyrifera within two decades. [1]

The IUCN listed B. sacra as near threatened in 1998, and frankincense trees are not covered by CITES.[1] Heavily tapped trees produce seeds that germinate at 16 percent versus over 80 percent for untapped trees, and B. serrata has been described as at risk from unsustainable harvesting.[1][13]
